newsitem.title: UK: BAe speechless on US strike fighter news.
newsitem.headline: BAe speechless on US strike fighter news.

text.p: British Aerospace Plc said on Monday it was disappointed its bid with McDonnell Douglas has been rejected for the potential $100 billion contract to build a new multi-service strike aircraft for the U.S.
But it declined to say whether it would now seek to use Britain's investment in the Joint Strike Fighter development programme to get work with the two finalists, or to make any further comment.
"There is very little that can be said at this moment other than that British Aerospace is disappointed at the announcement," a company spokesman said.
Consortia led by Lockheed Martin and Boeing were picked to go through to the final round of the contest on Saturday and will now build rival prototypes at a cost of a combined $2.2 billion.

The JSF program is intended to replace the F-16 fighter for the U.S. Air Force, the F/A-18 carrier-based fighter for the U.S. Navy and the Harrier AV-8B for the Marine Corps, which together promise a launch order for some 3,000 aircraft.

But the British government is investing $200 million in the prototype programme to participate in the Short-Take-Off, Vertical Landing (STOVL) version of the JSF for the Marine Corps as a possible replacement for its own Royal Navy Harriers.
The Royal Air Force is also considering a conventional takeoff version of the JSF in its studies for a Future Offensive Aircraft (FAO) to replace its Tornado GR4 strike aircraft.
Whether there is a role in JSF work for British Aerospace now its bid with McDonnell DOuglas has been dropped remains to be seen.

But Britain's defence procurement minister James Arbuthnot said in a statement on Saturday: "The winning consortia which already include substantial contributions from British companies, will now be permitted to restructure their industrial teams and we expect a significant share of the work to be carried out by British industry."
Other British firms are already involved in the winning consortia, including Rolls-Royce and GEC-Marconi.
"I think they (BAe) need to think out what they do next," said a political source on Monday.
